The authors developed a high-resolution additive manufacturing technique that uses upconversion nanoparticles and wavefront shaping to focus near-infrared light through highly scattering media.
Upconversion nanoparticles convert near-infrared light to ultraviolet light for photopolymerization and to visible light that is used as a guide star for wavefront shaping.
The authors used a digital micromirror device (DMD) to modulate the amplitude of the input light, rather than a liquid crystal spatial light modulator which modulates the phase.

The optical memory effect, where a shifted or tilted input wavefront results in an equally shifted or tilted output wavefront, was exploited to dynamically shift the focal spot through the scattering medium.
A nonlinearity parameter n of 2.4 was observed for the upconverted fluorescence signal at lower light intensities, indicating a multi-photon process.
Through the holographic diffuser, features as small as 1.5 μm were printed, while through the 300 μm thick chicken tissue, features as small as 2 μm were printed.
The FWHM of the optical memory effect was 16 μm for the holographic diffuser and 8 μm for the 300 μm thick chicken tissue.
Dynamic focusing, where the focal spot was shifted in 5 μm increments and the wavefront re-optimized, was used to maintain a uniform light dose during the printing process.
Printing through the chicken tissue showed more non-uniformity and over-polymerization in some regions, suggesting the need for real-time adjustment of the laser power and optimization parameters.
The optimization speed in the non-invasive configuration was limited by the low signal intensity from the back-scattered upconverted fluorescence.
The authors were able to print features that were over 5 times smaller than the speckle size within the scattering medium.
The authors demonstrated successful printing through both a holographic diffuser and a 300 μm thick slice of chicken breast tissue.
The authors note that the time required to focus light in their approach cannot exceed the ms range due to the dynamic nature of biological tissues.
The authors suggest that improving the upconversion efficiency of the nanoparticles and using more sensitive detectors could increase the optimization speed.
The authors were unable to pre-determine the absolute position of the printed voxels, as the global maximum of the focused spot could shift to different hot spots within the illuminated resin.
